new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is predictable from syllable weight within a three-syllable window at the right edge: a bimoraic final syllable (long vowel, or closed by two consonants or a geminate) takes stress; otherwise a bimoraic penult takes stress; if both final and penult are light, stress falls on the penult in disyllables and on the antepenult in longer words. The default (and by far most frequent) outcome is penultimate stress, with final stress on heavy finals. Jastrow 1997: 336 and Bergsträsser 1915: XXI state the same final-if-heavy-else-penult rule; Eid's corpus study adds the light-light antepenult case. Only one long vowel per word, always in the stressed syllable; unstressed (pretonic) vowels shorten and mid vowels raise.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Eid 2024 does not discuss secondary stress. Bergsträsser 1915: XX-XXI mentions a 'Gegenton' (counter-accent, marked with the same acute) in longer complexes but gives no rule.
new_statements.exceptions: Arnold 1990: 40-41, 328 notes CVCVCa loanwords with antepenult stress (sálaṭa 'salad', mákana 'car', sínama 'cinema'); Eid 2024: 215 finds ~70 antepenult-stressed word forms, not all loans, all with light penult and light final, and folds them into rule (4c). Bergsträsser 1915: XX notes sentence-level shifts (verb stressed on its final syllable before an immediately following object; proclitic/enclitic words lose stress).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; corpus word forms from the Maaloula Aramaic Speech Corpus (published texts of Arnold 1991a/b, Bergsträsser 1915 etc.). Phrase-level shifts and de-stressing of clitics described by Bergsträsser 1915: XX-XXI. All three statements are for the Ma'lula dialect; Jastrow 1997 frames the rule for WNA generally with Ma'lula examples.
new_statements.identity_note: All first-hand statements describe the Ma'lula (Maaloula) dialect of Western Neo-Aramaic [west2763 / amw]; Eid 2024 is explicitly Ma'lula-only (corpus of Ma'lula texts), Jastrow 1997 frames the rule for WNA as a whole with Ma'lula examples, Bergsträsser 1915 is Ma'lula. Bakh'a and Jubb'adin are covered only in Arnold 1990 (not opened). Glottolog attaches Maclean 1895 (NENA) and Jacobi 1973 (Turoyo) to this languoid in error; both are ignored here.

sources.note: The book's title page reads 'Grammar of the Dialects of Vernacular Syriac as spoken by the Eastern Syrians of Kurdistan, North-West Persia, and the Plain of Mosul, with notices of the vernacular of the Jews of Azerbaijan and of Zakhu near Mosul' - i.e. North-Eastern Neo-Aramaic (Urmi, Kurdistan, Mosul plain, Jewish Azerbaijani, Zakho), not the Western Neo-Aramaic of Maaloula/Bakh'a/Jubb'adin. Its penult-default rule is not evidence for west2763; Glottolog's attachment of this work to the languoid is a misattribution (already noted in the earlier reading).

sources.note: 'Word Stress' p. 336: 'Word stress is usually on the penultimate; the last syllable is stressed if it has a long vowel or ends in two or more consonants' (Ma. zappen 'he sold' vs zappén! 'sell!'); divergences marked with acute. Also: long vowels occur only in stressed syllables, so one long vowel per word.

sources.note: Einleitung p. XXI, §III.3: 'Der Akzent ist exspiratorisch. Die Tonsilbe ist.. leicht zu bestimmen: die letzte Silbe trägt den Ton, wenn sie langvokalig oder doppelt geschlossen ist, in allen übrigen Fällen die vorletzte; dabei gelten die zweiten Bestandteile von Diphthongen.. als Konsonanten.' Also notes a 'Gegenton' (counter-accent) and sentence-level shifts (verb stressed on final syllable before an immediately following object; unstressed proclitics/enclitics).
Nothing on stress; used only for its bibliography (pointed to Eid 2024 and the menadoc/Halle scans).
